criteria_quotes: Total shoulder arthroplasty may be considered medically necessary for joint disease when ALL of the following criteria are met: There is a documented diagnosis of one of the following: Degenerative joint disease (DJD), Osteoarthritis (OA), Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), Traumatic arthritis, Avascular necrosis AND Treatment is needed because of one or more of the following: Disabling pain for at least 3 months duration; Functional disability which interferes with the ability to carry out activities of daily living for at least 3 months duration AND Radiographic or imaging evidence (e.g., X-ray, CT, MRI) of destructive degenerative joint disease of the shoulder in the 12 months prior to surgery as evidenced by ONE or more of the following: Irregular joint surfaces, Glenoid sclerosis, Glenoid osteophyte changes, Flattened glenoid, Cystic changes in the humeral head, Joint space narrowing AND Documentation of three months of failed non-operative conservative management as demonstrated by a trial of one or more of the following: Anti-inflammatory medications or analgesics, Intra-articular injection of corticosteroids as appropriate AND A 6 week trial of one or more of the following physical measures under the direction of a healthcare professional: Physical therapy, Activity modification, Flexibility and muscle strengthening exercises

OR Total shoulder arthroplasty may be considered medically necessary for ANY of the following conditions: Proximal humerus fracture malunion or non-union; Reconstruction after tumor resection of the glenohumeral joint or surrounding tissue; Failed hemi-arthroplasty; Post-traumatic injury (e.g., fracture, infection) causing shoulder joint destruction
Total shoulder, reverse total shoulder, or hemi-arthroplasty is considered not medically necessary when the above medical necessity criteria are not met.

Documentation Requirements: For a total shoulder arthroplasty and degenerative joint disease such as osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis or traumatic arthritis or osteonecrosis ALL of the following are present: Needs treatment because of disabling pain and/or limited shoulder function interfering with activities of daily living (ADLs) AND Imaging evidence of destructive degenerative joint disease of the shoulder in the 12 months prior to surgery as evidenced by one or more of the following: irregular joint surfaces, glenoid sclerosis, glenoid osteophyte changes, flattened glenoid, cystic changes in the humeral head or joint space narrowing AND History of unsuccessful three-month trial of failed non-operative conservative management...
answer.appeal_deadline: 180 days from the date of the denial notice (2026-08-09), i.e., must be received by 2027-02-05, as stated both in the denial letter and in Premera's 'Your Complaint and Appeal Rights' document.
answer.submission_route: Submit a written appeal using Premera's Member Appeal form, or a letter, mailed to: Premera Blue Cross, Attn: Member Appeals, P.O. Box 91102, Seattle, WA 98111-9202. Alternatively, fax to the Appeals Department at 425-918-5592. You may also call Customer Service at 1-800-722-1471 for help or to request an expedited review if a delay would harm your health. If the internal appeal is denied again, Premera must provide information about further appeal rights, including an Independent Review Organization (IRO) external review, and Washington residents may also contact the WA Office of the Insurance Commissioner (1-800-562-6900) for assistance with a Fully Insured plan.
answer.how_to_obtain_criteria: The full policy 7.01.590 'Shoulder Arthroplasty' (PDF) is publicly posted on Premera's medical policy website and was retrieved directly at the URL above. The patient/provider should submit imaging reports, clinical notes documenting duration and severity of pain/functional disability, and records of at least 3 months of conservative treatment (medications/injections) and a 6-week supervised PT/activity-modification trial to address the specific criteria the denial cites as unmet ('imaging findings ... do not support medical necessity').
answer.notes: The denial letter cites CPT 23472 (total shoulder arthroplasty, non-fracture indication implied) and states the imaging findings do not support medical necessity — this maps directly to the imaging-evidence bullet in the 'joint disease' pathway of Policy 7.01.590 (one or more of: irregular joint surfaces, glenoid sclerosis, glenoid osteophyte changes, flattened glenoid, cystic changes in the humeral head, joint space narrowing, within 12 months prior to surgery). To win the appeal, the submitted imaging report and radiologist interpretation should explicitly document at least one of these six findings, and the medical record should also independently document disabling pain/functional disability duration and the required conservative-treatment trials, since the denial letter only flags the imaging piece but the payer will look at the whole policy on appeal. One caveat: the policy's effective date (April 1, 2026) is after the plan year start but before the November 2026 denial date, so it is very likely the version applied to this specific prior-authorization determination — however, Premera revises these policies periodically, so if the request was actually reviewed under an earlier version of 7.01.590, the patient/provider should ask Premera in writing (or via the appeal) to confirm the exact policy version and effective date used for this specific denial, since Premera does not appear to publicly archive superseded versions of this document online.

Introduction Shoulder arthroplasty is when surgery is performed to replace the shoulder joint. The damaged part of the shoulder joint is removed, and metal and plastic parts are put in its place. A common reason for people to need this surgery is very bad pain from overuse, and not being able to do normal daily activities. Some people may need only a part of their shoulder replaced, which is when the shoulder head or ball is replaced with metal or plastic parts, but the socket is left as is. Sometimes the implanted parts need to be reversed. This is called reverse shoulder arthroplasty. This policy outlines when shoulder arthroplasty may be considered medically necessary. Note: The Introduction section is for your general knowledge and is not to be taken as policy coverage criteria.
